analysis.one_liner: Repeals the health reform rule barring insurers from denying coverage to adults with preexisting conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on November 29, 2010, and never received a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal a provision of the 2010 health care law (the Affordable Care Act) that stops health insurers from refusing to cover adults because of a preexisting condition, such as cancer, diabetes, or a past illness. If it had passed, insurers could again deny coverage to, or charge far higher prices to, adults with health conditions. The bill was introduced by Rep. Gary Ackerman (D-NY) with no cosponsors and was referred to committee, where it died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, health insurers would have gained the ability to again exclude or charge more to adults with preexisting conditions, lowering their costs by keeping the sickest customers out of their risk pools. People with health conditions would have borne the cost, either through higher premiums or being unable to buy coverage at all.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the ACA provision barring group and individual health plans from imposing preexisting condition exclusions on adults 19 and older, effective immediately upon enactment.
It removes ACA protections against discrimination based on health status for adult enrollees, giving insurers back the ability to turn away or price out people with health conditions.

analysis.who_pays: Adults with preexisting conditions — cancer survivors, people with diabetes, asthma, or heart disease — would pay through denial of coverage or sharply higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the preexisting condition protections would again allow insurers to deny coverage or charge unaffordable prices to adults with conditions like cancer, diabetes, or pregnancy — the people who most need insurance.
The repeal is written to take effect as of its own enactment, meaning adults with preexisting conditions would lose the ACA's protection immediately, not on any gradual phase-in.
The bill targets only the adult protections; it does not address how the individual insurance market would function for high-cost enrollees if exclusions return.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a clear benefit for insurers — freedom to price or deny coverage to sick adults — but those benefits come directly at the cost of coverage for the very people least able to afford insurance on the open market. There is no counterweight benefit to ordinary people in the bill's text. It never advanced, so the costs and benefits were never seriously weighed in Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Ackerman (D-NY) introduced the bill on November 29, 2010, about eight months after the ACA became law.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced; no further action was taken.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without ever receiving a committee markup or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The ACA's protections for adults with preexisting conditions remained on the books, so people with health conditions kept the ability to buy insurance. No one gained from the bill's death beyond the status quo.

for.name: Rep. Gary Ackerman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ACA's ban on preexisting condition exclusions for adults.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and never reached a vote, so no party-line pattern on the merits can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would restore insurers' ability to deny coverage or charge far more to adults with preexisting conditions, which reduces their costs by excluding the sickest and most expensive patients. If it had become law, people with health conditions would again struggle to buy coverage at any price.

Roughly a large share of adults have a health condition that insurers could treat as a preexisting condition; the repeal would remove the ACA's guarantee that they can buy coverage regardless of health status.
